The scenario harness's `observe.pool_shape()` probe had a `timeout N cd <dir> && find ...` bug: `timeout` cannot exec the `cd` shell-builtin, so `&&` short-circuited and the probe silently returned no `_total`; fixed to `timeout N sh -c '<cd && find | xargs stat>'`.

RustFS stores each object as a directory containing an `xl.meta` file plus erasure part files (MinIO-style layout), which is the source of the roughly 2.2x on-disk store amplification observed relative to distinct payload size.

A CA-s3 stateless-test baseline attribution ran the 38 CA-s3-lane FAILs on the normal non-CA job: 31 also failed there (local-env noise, not CA-caused), leaving 7 CA-specific failures — 3 promote-vs-GC-condemn ABORTED, 2 timeouts, 1 TTL diff, 1 write-path memory issue — of which the 3 ABORTED were the meaningful production-robustness class.

A backlogged protocol optimization (PROMOTE-REVALIDATION-MINIMIZATION): the ack-floor model licenses skipping per-leaf promote HEADs when the installed round is unchanged since dependency observation (`DepEntry::observed_view_round`), complementary to the resurrect fixes which cover the recovery path when the round moved mid-commit.

Deep read-path profiling in the campaign found `DownloadPart` (relink fetch) is the dominant read cost: 28.7k fetches cost 1.02M GET + 1.96M HEAD requests despite zero blob re-upload, driven by per-file `loadMeta` GET plus occupancy/adopt HEAD; the identified optimization lever is manifest-trust adoption without per-file probes.

An uncertainty-exhaustion abort class was identified as a backlog item: `putBlob`'s pre-existing 8-round ABORTED loop times the ~90s controller budget can reach roughly 12 minutes worst case, crossing the native `receive_timeout` (300s) around round 3-4 and causing client-side ambiguity; the fix direction is a distinct "uncertainty budget exhausted" abort class that stops the outer ABORTED loop from re-driving a fully exhausted controller envelope.

A full CA-s3 lane post-mortem exonerated the B86 log-policy removal for the observed timeout growth: ProfileEvents on every stalled query showed zero CAS/RustFS wait, with threads parked on HTTP socket reads to public internet buckets (e.g. `clickhouse-datasets-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com`) — the timeouts were external internet weather, not a CA regression.

CAS GC's `gc_fold_begin`/`gc_fold_end` audit rows write only an anomaly count (e.g. `{anomalies: '1'}`) as `detail`; `recordAnomaly` takes namespace, shard, manifest and reason but none of it reaches the audited row, so a firing cannot be identified or distinguished from other anomaly classes after the fact.

CAS probe A (the ref-scan disagreement detector) reports each hole with the ref-log id and its direction: holes missing from the fold's own (second) scan are explainable by concurrent deletion, but holes missing from the pre-fold (first) scan are not — the object existed at the second walk and its id sits below what the first walk had already observed, so the first walk should have returned it.

fsck's `corrupted_runs` finding was invisible on the fsck summary and treated as non-fatal even though it is a `clean()` term; separately the entry-gate fsck budget was inverted (subprocess timeout 180s vs scan deadline 600s), making the `--partial` degrade path unreachable from the harness, and 4 of 39 checkpoints in a 4h soak lost their whole fsck gate as a result.

Turning on fsck's `--partial` degrade path without further changes would fabricate a consistency proof: a timed-out scan returns `dangling=0`, and the soak harness's `wait_for_pool_consistent` counts that fabricated zero as a clean read; the remaining `FsckTimeout` path still substitutes fabricated zeros and is tracked as BACKLOG `{#fsck-fabricated-clean-on-timeout}`, a landmine guarded today only because every consumer happens to check first.

A production regression where a stateless test (`05008`) went red was traced to `UniversePolicy::kDefault == StageA_Suppressed`, which suppresses destructive GC on every production round; the introducing commit swept 20+ gtest files and touched zero files under `tests/queries/`, so its stateless-test blast radius was invisible to its own test run.

A retry path that treats a vanished CAS catalog object as an empty catalog is a silent-default-substitution defect: on retry after a vanish, it would replace every namespace's catalog with a single mutation's output via create-if-absent; the in-tree analogue `PoolMeta::admitOrValidate` already fails closed on exactly that observation and was cited as the pattern to follow.

CA gtest scratch directories leaked at scale — about 50,000 `CasGtestScratch`-family directories exhausted a 1.048M-inode tmpfs and broke an unrelated build; swept the affected suites from ~100% leaking to 14%, with the remaining teardown fix chartered as BACKLOG `[CA-GTEST-TMP-SCRATCH-LEAK]` and deliberately not run while other lane gates are in flight.

CAS's `RefLaneState` (`Ready`, `Writing`, `Wedged`, `NeedsRecovery`, `Closed`, `Faulted`) replaces the earlier nested apply-marker/durable-floor/wedge encoding because that encoding COMPOSED independent decisions rather than selecting among alternatives, so a TLA+ exhaustiveness argument built as a product of those dimensions bounded nothing — the same reasoning defect (a dimension computed from another) independently recurred in an unrelated C++ chain-link invariant sweep.

Under CAS's `RefLaneState` model, relink certification is Ready-state-only: a resumed relink gate consumes a single-state precondition instead of the twelve-row cross-product the earlier encoding required, and the NETWORK_ERROR/terminal split means only `Closed`/`Faulted` are non-retriable while all other states retry.

CAS's transient-vs-terminal exception classifier separates a READ-plane and a WRITE-plane per an audit of every throw site tree-wide: the READ plane is the only one with destructive reach and had exactly two sites, of 106 GC-ref throw sites tree-wide 27 were transient (19 `NETWORK_ERROR`, 5 `INVALID_STATE`, 3 `ABORTED`); a write-once `ABORTED`-on-write-once site (718 occurrences) was judged a real defect while the deposition/fence family was deliberately left `INVALID_STATE` because recoding it to `ABORTED` would regress by escaping a backoff exemption.

A transient CA lease loss could be misclassified by the part-check thread as "part looks broken" and trigger destructive-shaped remediation; root-caused via correlated CA-log/part_log/text_log traces and fixed by pinning `TransientRefusalIsUpstreamRetryableTerminalIsNot` to call the real `isRetryableException` on both true and false branches, live-validated by reproducing the same blip against the fixed binary and observing zero "looks broken" lines.

A destructive GC gate based only on `proven == total` accepts an empty universe vacuously because `0 == 0`; the fix adds an explicit nonempty-authority predicate so the gate cannot be satisfied by having nothing to prove.

CAS's `contentAddressedFsckColumns` SQL row (the `SYSTEM ... FSCK` output) does not surface `lifeless_keys` even though the function's own comment states every term of `FsckReport::clean` must appear there; the comment claiming the summary is derived mechanically from `clean()`'s field set was false — the actual implementation is five hand-listed field names, so the enforcement mechanism the comment describes does not exist.

A `LOGICAL_ERROR`-under-sanitizer abort class gets a mandatory review trigger on its fifth recurrence in one week across the CAS codebase, requiring a file-wide grep sweep, because such an abort hides every subsequent test in the same process from running.

D2 classified S31 (ca-gc-dryrun under gc_shards>1) as INFRA: `docker-compose-gc_shards2.yml up -d` returned rc=1 and the cluster never became healthy within 240s, producing 0/0 verdicts (errored at reset) rather than executing any test.

D2 found S21 (read-heavy many-ref) failed because the test ran `SELECT ... FINAL` against a plain `ReplicatedMergeTree`, producing `ILLEGAL_FINAL` on 12/48 queries, and separately its column-prune check (`1col=0 all=0`) was vacuous at dev scale because blobs were fully cached; recommended fix is to drop FINAL or use a ReplacingMergeTree and gate column-prune at a scale where blobs aren't fully cached.

D2 found S20 (replicated fetch and relink) failed because the follower's `CasRootCas` counter read 0, noting the CAS counters may not be scoped per-node; recommended fix is to scope the CAS counter per node or make the verdict record-only.

D2 found S10 (patch parts + lightweight deletes) left a deleted bucket with 60 rows and patch parts observed = 0 (which may merge away quickly); classified as SCALE/TIMING, recommending verification at bigger scale with sync/settle before the count rather than treating it as a product bug.

D2 deferred S23's 1-server and 10-server idle baselines as INCONCLUSIVE pending multi-topology infra (tied to the S12 10-replica Cluster node-count backlog), and flagged S23's idle RSS at +82 MiB against a 64 MiB budget as likely allocator/log slack requiring confirmation it does not grow unbounded during the 4h soak.

codex_r6_findings.md's 'Checks that held' section confirms: a ref-log body whose decoded sequence differs from its key is already rejected; under a true state-derived next ID a dying lane that sees a seal at T+1 cannot create T+2 and must retry T+1; seal-on-every-transition (including clean transitions) is stated correctly; the S42 removal-tail retention rule is safety-correct (its missing piece is bounded execution, finding 6); and REBUILD condemn-nothing fixes the round-5 asymmetric-LIST data-loss scenario (its missing piece is orphan-blob reclamation, finding 9).

codex_r6_findings.md's round-5 disposition table maps all 10 round-5 review findings against the v6 ref-chain redesign: fully resolved (later definite result after ambiguity; clean-transition sealing), resolved for safety only (REBUILD condemnation; cross-epoch removals), partially resolved (recovery snapshot authority; one enumeration/falsifiability), unresolved (namespace incarnation; current-epoch manifest bodies; catalog partial transitions/capacity), and resolved for the original mismatch only (CAS-walk controller mismatch) — each disposition cites which of the 13 new v6 findings covers the remaining gap. Overall verdict: REJECT.

S23's initial idle-RSS-growth failure correlated with elevated S3 error rates in the same window (read 8.6%, write 17.2% on one node); S3 retries allocate transient upload/download buffers that jemalloc keeps resident as dirty pages, inflating RSS without inflating tracked memory, which is one of two identified amplifiers of the outlier (the other being fresh-boot warmup variance).

The D1 1h chaos soak ran with `CA_SOAK_NO_HARD_KILL=1`, which deterministically downgrades a hard `docker kill` fault on a CH replica to a graceful RESTART, because S13 exposed that a hard-killed CA server cannot currently self-recover its mount.

Round-1 remedy disposition verdicts for the ref-chain recovery redesign (from the round-2 review): seal high-water adoption sound but void precedence unusable without authoritative interval discovery (REFUTE in part); monotone rebirth sound but permanent per-fold-seal tombstone embedding rejected (REFUTE); zero `sealed_from` alone cannot encode a never-born namespace (REFUTE); pin only recovery seals, not every snapshot above cursor (REFUTE the broader pin); shared intake primitive upheld but non-cut-scoped B1/B2 accounting rejected (REFUTE); mutator inventory upheld but restart without a sticky required-coverage floor rejected (REFUTE); fsck `unchecked` principle upheld but must be whole-run without a universe/quiescence proof; "may refuse after exceeding" pending-liveness bound rejected (REFUTE) as not a bound; ID hygiene UPHELD provided allocation uses a saturating atomic CAS that never wraps the shared counter.

The current fsck oracle assumes a snapshot ID is also a log ID and silently skips a recovery seal on that assumption, rather than reporting the skip as checked; and repeated per-held-namespace anchor/repair GETs on every folding round are rate-bounded only by the scheduler, with no cumulative bound or backoff.

`rebuildBaseline` (`cas-gc-rebuild`) has no mount-lease interlock: a live server's fresh mount lease does not stop rebuild from performing, because the tool's only live-server guard is the caller's own `isReadOnly()` flag, which cannot see a server mounted read-write on another host — contrasted with `LeaseConflictRefuses`, which does refuse on a GC-lease conflict. Confirmed as a real bug by the feature owner ("Yep, this looks real... gc-rebuild i've added recently, and it almost untested"). A regression test `CasGcRebuild.GCR1_NoMountLeaseInterlock_RunsUnderLiveMount` demonstrates rebuild running under a live mount; the fix flips the assertion to `EXPECT_FALSE(rep.performed)` with a mount-related refusal string.

`Build::promote` can overwrite an existing committed ref (`refs[dst]=T_a`) with a new manifest (`T_b`) without releasing `T_a`, permanently orphaning (leaking) the old manifest and its blobs; this is the most concrete confirmed storage leak from the review. Fix: `Build::promote` must, when `refs[R]` already names another manifest, either emit a proper committed-to-committed repoint or fail closed with an exception; also move `Build::abandon`'s `retireBuildSeq` call after the removal mutation.

CAS's single true read-side correctness hole (labeled X1/R1, "missing read"): a ref-less/cross-node reader resolves ref to manifest to blob-location at plan time, discards the manifest, then performs a deferred, unpinned blob GET later; if the ref is dropped and GC completes condemn to pending to delete before that GET fires, a committed datum becomes unreadable mid-query (`NoSuchKey`). This is bounded to the write/GC plane being otherwise loss-free; the fix direction is an ephemeral reader pin folded into the GC mark/ack-floor union, or bounding query lifetime below the condemn-to-delete latency.

CAS's single-shard `RootShard` register is linearizable only while single-writer holds, because the shard `casPut` is fenced by a content token, not a monotone `writer_epoch`; a paused/superseded writer (J1), a VM clone sharing `server_uuid` (J2), or wall-clock lease-expiry-vs-boot-clock skew (J3) each open a dual-writer window that produces split-brain / zombie-value / non-linearizable / forked-journal-history anomalies. This is the single headline register-level finding of the Jepsen/Elle-style consistency audit; the fix is to carry `writer_epoch` into the shard-CAS precondition, the same reject-if-stale pattern GC already uses on its `deleteExact`/`gc/state` CAS (which is why GC leadership is already split-brain-safe).

A persistent shard clamp halts all GC reclamation pool-wide (G-N1): GC's fail-closed uncertainty handling means one unresolved anomaly stops reclamation everywhere, not just for the affected shard; the recommended fix keeps the fail-closed behavior but adds observability and an operator escape (clamp age, clamped key/shard, alerting, documented fsck/rebuild path), with scoped suppression deferred as a later option.

A coalesced shard read (single-flight read coalescing) has no deadline (F-N1): if the leader's GET hangs, all coalesced follower readers block indefinitely (a reader convoy) — a real liveness finding distinct from any correctness issue.

ReplicatedMergeTree/CAS ref divergence on partial commit (RPL-2): ZooKeeper is the source of truth for the part set while CAS refs are the source of truth for bytes, and these are two independent commit points with no cross-transaction. If a replica adds a part to ZK but crashes before the CAS ref promote lands, the part is "known" but `resolveRef` returns absent, triggering a re-fetch (recoverable). The converse (CAS-has/ZK-missing) produces an orphaned live ref: reachable and keeping its blobs alive, but invisible to the table — a silent storage leak until DROP TABLE reclaims the namespace.

Relink races GC in the shared pool (RPL-3): between the sender encoding a manifest and the receiver's `promote`, GC on the shared pool can condemn a blob that was live via the sender's ref; this is a TOCTOU inside promote in the same window as the general J1 zombie-writer/X1 reader-pin class, mitigated in practice by GC's two-phase graduation (`delete_pending` before `deleteExact`) plus copy-forward, but not provably closed for the relink promote path and has no dedicated test.

`to_detached` relink is disabled and `FETCH PARTITION` always streams bytes (RPL-4): the receiver only advertises relink when `try_zero_copy && !to_detached`, so `ALTER TABLE ... FETCH PARTITION` (into `detached/`) and the byte-fetch fallback never relink — they stream full bytes even within the same pool, then content-address and dedup on landing. This is correct but a performance cliff, explicitly deferred in code as "Relink-into-detached is a deferred optimization".

Quorum inserts, `SYSTEM SYNC REPLICA`, lost-replica recovery (`cloneReplica`), and `REPLACE_RANGE`/`DROP_RANGE` log entries all reduce to sequences of fetch (relink or byte) plus drop against a CA disk, but there is no integration test exercising them, and `cloneReplica` in particular can enqueue a large fan-out of GETs that each should relink and crosses the RPL-3/RPL-4 risk classes (RPL-5).

The content-hash algorithm (CityHash128) is an unversioned, unpinned pool contract (AD1-3): a future change to the hash algorithm would silently fork dedup and break relink, because nothing pins or versions which hash algorithm a pool's content-addressed keys were computed with.

The identity/fencing model has three durable layers with a fixed startup order: `OwnerProto`/owner is identity (write-once binding of `server_root_id` to `server_uuid`, clock-free, never deleted or reassigned, foreign UUID fails closed even if a lease is expired); `ServerEpochProto`/epoch is the durable monotone fence (CAS-bumped on each mount attempt, hands out a fresh `writer_epoch`, must survive lease expiry/reclaim, and a missing epoch over non-empty data is a reset hazard); `MountLeaseProto`/mount is liveness (renewed repeatedly, has wall-clock expiry/seq/hostname/pid diagnostics, reclaimable when expired or GC-fenced). Startup order is exactly owner then epoch then mount.

`part_manifest_cleanup` (`FoldSealProto.part_manifest_cleanup`, `Layout::partManifestCleanupKey`, `Gc::writePartManifestCleanupBundle`) is a written-but-never-read artifact left over from an unfinished sharded-GC design that was superseded by the one-pass ack-floor GC (commit `774404eb3dc`, 2026-07-02): the bundle is written on every fold but no runtime reader was found that applies it, and actual manifest-body deletion instead happens post-CAS directly from in-memory `folded.mf_cleanup`; if the process crashes in that post-CAS window, recovery goes through the orphan-manifest sweep, not the persisted cleanup bundle. Recommendation: either delete the dead write path and its tests, or implement a real recovery reader that replays exact manifest deletes from the bundle after an adopted fold seal.

`kMutablePerPartFiles` was renamed to `kPerRefPartFiles` (with per-file rationale documented): `txn_version.txt` is genuinely mutable in-place (MVCC rewrites it after part publication) and stays a per-ref mutable sidecar; `uuid.txt` and `metadata_version.txt` are not mutated in-place under the single-owner-manifest model and were reclassified as ordinary immutable part files inside the manifest rather than sidecars, since the old dual-part-ref-sharing-one-manifest rationale for excluding them no longer applies once CAS stages a fresh `ManifestId` per ref.

CAS's security perimeter is exactly the S3 bucket credential: there is no intra-pool authorization, identities are self-asserted and unsigned, and blobs are shared pool-wide by content hash with no namespace in the blob key. Combined with non-cryptographic CityHash128 content-addressing and reads that never re-verify payload-against-key, this enables SEC-1 (High) collision poisoning: because dedup is HEAD-first and blobs are pool-global, an attacker who can craft a `CityHash128` collision can pre-seed a poisoned blob under the victim's future hash so a victim in a different table/tenant later writing the benign content dedups to the poison and reads attacker bytes, with all CRC checks passing (latent in a single-trust-domain pool, real the moment a pool is multi-tenant).

`cas-gc-rebuild`'s security verdict: it cannot delete live data directly (deletions still flow through the normal round's ack-floor plus two-phase plus exact-token path), and a crafted owner state that makes rebuild under-count requires full owner-plane write access, which already implies total pool compromise (SEC-3) — the trimmed-history guard closes the naive truncation path. Residual risks: FORCE only skips the healthy-pool check (operational risk, not a safety bypass); rebuild does a full-universe discover-and-fold (O(all shards + all journals)), an expensive pool-wide sweep an attacker with SYSTEM access could trigger repeatedly (shares the SEC-4 decode/fold exhaustion surface); and a concurrent GC leader's round CAS and rebuild's `gc/state` install can contend, so rebuild must be verified to respect GC leadership or a split-baseline is possible.

CAS's documented deployment rule from the security audit: never share a CAS pool across trust domains until SEC-1 (collision poisoning), SEC-2 (dedup existence oracle), and SEC-3 (no intra-pool authorization) are addressed; the single highest-leverage code fix common to both the Jepsen-style consistency audit and the security audit is a `writer_epoch`-fenced shard CAS precondition, which simultaneously closes SEC-7 (NTP/pause-amplifiable fencing) and the J1/J2/J3 split-brain class.

The reviewer's (Mikhail) final disposition of the review findings: most "findings" and comments were judged not real or by-design, with a small set treated as genuine and prioritized: (1) GCR-1 rebuild mount-lease interlock — real, add the interlock; (2) `Build::promote` overwrite leak — the most concrete storage leak, fix by failing closed or repointing; (3) lost-ACK idempotency (W-N1/W-N2/J5) — reconcile by reading post-state instead of blindly replaying; (4) J1/J2/J3 writer-lease-is-not-a-fencing-token — add a SIGSTOP/SIGCONT test first, then re-check `mayMutate` immediately before the shard CAS as a short-term mitigation, `writer_epoch`-in-precondition as the longer-term fix; (5) G-N1 persistent clamp — keep fail-closed but add observability/operator escape. RPL-3 was judged safe in practice because the sender cannot remove a part until it receives an ack, which the receiver gives only after a successful write.

SEC-4: a pool-write-capable party (or a corrupt/huge object) can place a valid-CRC, valid-framing but enormous shard or manifest directly in S3; decoders (`decodeRootShard`, `decodePartManifest`) validate magic/version/CRC/journal-integrity but a valid giant body still allocates on decode, causing OOM in readers and the GC folder (GC folds whole journals). Recommendation: enforce absolute decode-side size/element caps independent of the write path, and stream large journals in the fold.

SEC-5: key builders route through `checkNamespace`, `namespaceFileKey`, and `mountpointObjectKey`, which reject empty segments, the reserved `_files`/`_manifests`/`_precommits` names, `..`, leading/trailing `/`, and `//`, but `checkNamespace` itself does not reject a `..` segment; this is safe only because the backend is an object store with literal (non-normalized) keys, so a filesystem-backed or path-normalizing backend would be vulnerable to traversal. Recommendation: reject `..` in `checkNamespace` so the invariant does not silently depend on backend key semantics.

SEC-7: the write/GC audit's fencing findings (J1/J2/J3) are attacker-amplifiable — an attacker who can skew a victim's clock via unauthenticated NTP can force a premature mount-lease reclaim and induce split-brain (J3), and an attacker who can induce a long stop-the-world pause (resource exhaustion, cgroup throttling) widens the unfenced `mayMutate()` to `casPut` window for a zombie write (J1); TLS protects S3 transit but NTP is typically unauthenticated. Recommendation: carry `writer_epoch` into the shard-CAS precondition, and require authenticated time (NTS/authenticated NTP) in deployment guidance.

SEC-8: provenance (`server_id`, timestamp, op, `build_id`) and the `CasEvent` sink give a useful audit trail, but everything is self-asserted and forgeable by a pool-write adversary, so it is good for debugging and honest-fault forensics but not an integrity/attribution control against a malicious insider.

SEC-9: blobs are plaintext table bytes; confidentiality relies entirely on S3 SSE + bucket policy + TLS, and content-addressing also makes content equality externally observable (same content maps to the same key), which deployments with confidential data across tenants in one pool should assume as an equality-leakage risk.

The DoS/amplification risk of `SYSTEM CONTENT ADDRESSED GC REBUILD` (SEC-6): rebuild does a full-universe discover-and-fold, O(all shards + all journals), so an attacker with SYSTEM privilege (or who can trigger repeated failures that tempt operators to rebuild) can make it an expensive, pool-wide, memory-heavy sweep sharing SEC-4's decode/fold exhaustion surface; recommended mitigation is rate-limiting/single-flight on the command plus streaming the fold.

The reviewer verified that rebuild adds no attack surface beyond SEC-3's total-compromise bar: an adversary who crafts an internally consistent owner state with refs silently removed could get rebuild to compute a baseline missing those edges, but the trimmed-history baseline guard detects truncated journals and fails closed, so producing an exploitable crafted state already requires full owner-plane write access (already total compromise). Residual open items: confirm the REBUILD RBAC grant is dedicated/narrow (not bundled into a broad SYSTEM grant), and confirm rebuild runs under GC leadership so it cannot race a live round into a split-baseline.

Reviewer (Mikhail) disposition on J3 (clock-skew reclaim): the CAS protocol is mostly clock-free already and could be made fully clock-free, but doing so would likely require waiting roughly 30-60 seconds while mounting the disk, and it is not clear that price is a good tradeoff versus keeping the wall-clock lease-expiry mechanism.

Reviewer disposition: the security finding labeled "SEC-2 - no intra-pool authz" in the reviewer's reply (matching the audit's SEC-3, no intra-pool authorization) is accepted as by-design: all bucket-credential holders share the same trust boundary. RPL-2 (ZK/CAS ref divergence on partial commit) is judged not a CAS-specific issue but general ReplicatedMergeTree partial-commit behavior that the project already knows how to resolve (via detached-parts handling). RPL-4 (`to_detached` relink disabled, always streams bytes) is accepted as a possible real performance issue to recheck, believed to use the same mechanics as a normal fetch. RPL-5 (no dedicated CAS integration tests for quorum/SYNC REPLICA/cloneReplica) is accepted as coverage debt comparable to other ClickHouse features, mitigated by all stateless tests passing successfully against a CAS-backed server.

RPL-3 disposition (relink races GC in the shared pool): judged safe in practice because while the sender is transmitting the part and has not received an acknowledgment from the receiver, the sender cannot remove the part; the receiver gives an acknowledgment only after a successful write.

A follow-up triage of the review (deduplicated against Mikhail's comments) sorted the "Verify / Add Tests" bucket into: (1) R1/X1 reader-vs-GC race — for normal MergeTree this is likely covered by DataPart lifetime; action is to document that CAS read safety depends on MergeTree part lifetime and audit whether any ref-less/cross-node reader path actually exists, implementing ephemeral read pins only if such a path is real; (2) replication paths — add CA-specific reconciliation tests for RPL-2 if cheap, add a targeted relink-vs-GC test for RPL-3, recheck the to_detached perf cliff for RPL-4, and treat RPL-5 as coverage debt; (3) W-N3 write-batching liveness — add queue-wait/leader-flush-latency/batch-size/batch-failure metrics first, then make the wait cancellation/timeout-aware only if the numbers show stalls.

The same follow-up triage sorted the "Document / Defer" bucket into: (1) security model — SEC-1 (CityHash128 not cryptographic) is the real concern if a pool crosses trust domains; for release, explicitly document "one CAS pool = one trust domain", and for multi-tenant future add a cryptographic hash mode or trust-domain-scoped dedup, with SEC-2/SEC-3 accepted as by-design under that model; (2) a day-2 runbook (AD-3) should be a table of failure mode to signal/metric to diagnostic command to recovery command to test, covering stalled GC, persistent clamp, lost/corrupt gc/state, live-mount conflict, orphan refs/manifests, pool-meta corruption, and backup/restore of the CAS control plane; (3) low/minor cleanup items R2-R4, W-N4, G-N2 through G-N4, SEC-4/SEC-5 are not urgent correctness blockers but good hardening: cache the manifest under the GET token, assert TTL vs GC latency, configure S3 multipart-cleanup lifecycle, add decode-size caps, and reject `..` in `checkNamespace`.

The follow-up triage's "Close As No-Action / By Design" bucket: G-N3 (spurious ABORTED on lost-ACK round CAS) is a false positive because the next GC round reads the already-committed `gc/state`; cross-shard serializability findings (fractured read, read skew, phantoms) are accepted as by-design; and RPL-2 (ZK/CAS ref divergence) should follow ReplicatedMergeTree's existing detached-part/recovery semantics rather than invent CAS-only cross-registry transactionality.

The full set of code sites sharing the renameParts -> Keeper-decision -> parts-commit slot audited for the part-durability-before-Keeper-commit fix is: `ReplicatedMergeTreeSink::commitPart` (INSERT, the only dedup-token site and hence the only silent-loss path), `renameMergedTemporaryPart` (merges), `MutateFromLogEntryTask::finalize`, `fetchPart`, `executeLogEntry`, `executeReplaceRange`, `replacePartitionFromImpl`, `movePartitionToTable`, `renameAndCommitEmptyParts`, and `createEmptyPartInsteadOfLost`; non-INSERT paths hit the same window but only cause replicated-log-entry re-execution churn, not acknowledged data loss.

The Stage B strategic-review concentration proposal's replacement namespace-removal sequence is: (1) catalog transitions Live to Removing; (2) the fenced owner appends the terminal record; (3) GC folds the terminal record and performs one bounded cleanup pass; (4) GC writes a stable retirement marker derived only from RootNamespace; (5) GC durably publishes a fold seal with that namespace's cursor pruned; (6) GC exact-deletes `_ckpt`; (7) catalog entry deletion happens last.

Ordering the retirement marker before `_ckpt` deletion means even catalog loss cannot turn a namespace-removal window into a fresh birth; creation must check both the retirement marker and the namespace's `_ckpt` by exact key before admission and refuse if either exists; a listing omission can leak old objects but cannot make a retired namespace visible again because it is never re-admitted.

Even under the no-namespace-reuse simplification, catalog authority, the `Creating` publication exclusion, the `Removing` positive-ownership exclusion, the exact-next frontier probe, durable holds, and the delete-site in-degree re-read must not be cut, because they prevent data loss independently of rebirth; a temporary "refuse while old objects survive, retry after GC" rule does not substitute for them since LIST cannot certify old-object absence.

If a deadline cannot absorb the four Stage-B simplification tasks (no-reuse contract + retirement marker, removing NamespaceLifeId/incarnation plumbing, concentrating lifecycle decisions in CasRefCatalog, and the shortened removal sequence) plus the destructive-gate soak, the only defensible fallback is to ship with `UniversePolicy` still suppressing destructive GC rather than hurriedly landing the existing incarnation-based Task 5 and flipping Task 7b.

The GC round's exact durable key layout: `gc/state` (controller state, one per pool, strict fail-closed CAGT-magic proto), `gc/hb` (advisory heartbeat, fixed 24-byte binary), `gc/gen/<g>/attempt/<a>/fold_seal` (write-once fold seal), `gc/gen/<g>/attempt/<a>/.../<round>/<shard>` (retire outcome log), `cas/refs/<ns>/_log/<txn_id>` (ref log txn), `cas/refs/<ns>/_snap/<id>.proto` (ref snapshot).

The ref state machine's load-bearing invariant is that `promote` never silently displaces a different committed row for the same name; a silent displacement would never emit the evicted manifest's -1 edge, leaking it phantom-alive forever. `stateFromSnapshot` round-trips a hand-built snapshot through the codec so the same bug class cannot enter via snapshot loading.

Blob reachability is source-edge set membership, not a counter: one source edge is (BlobRef, source_id) where source_id = CityHash128(namespace + ref + path), with 0 reserved as the sentinel key for kCondemned rows. The edge set is idempotent under re-fold, so retries and competing attempts produce byte-identical runs.

"Spared" means a condemned blob's in-degree recovered because a publish re-referenced it; the retired entry is dropped and recovery wins even past the graduation floor. "Forgotten" has no live meaning in this subsystem — the memory-noted GForget/GcSnap::forget design is superseded by pruneSupersededGenerations (wholesale generation retention).

`GcState::fence_seq` is dead protocol state: it is incremented on every lease steal and encoded/decoded/surfaced in `CasInspect`, but is read by no live protocol decision — keying moved to `(snap_generation, snap_attempt)`. `CasGcOutcomes.h`'s key-layout comment is stale, still documenting the old fence_seq-based outcome key instead of the real `outcomesKey(generation, attempt, round, shard)`.

A single-crash leak window exists in the GC round's Task-7 hand-off: the retention cursor can advance past a still-referenced generation while the post-CAS hand-off delete is only best-effort, so a crash between the CAS and the hand-off leaks a whole `gc/gen/<g>/` prefix until fsck reclaims it.

`suppress_destructive` (`!report.anomalies.empty()`) is independently recomputed in both `Gc::fold` and `Gc::runRegularRound`, coupled only through a mutable `report.anomalies`; if future code appends an anomaly between the two reads, the two decisions could silently diverge (fold suppresses deletes but the round doesn't, or vice versa).

There are two independent sharding axes in GC that are deliberately different and easy to confuse: `blobShard` (blob-hash high64 % gc_shards, for in-degree work) versus `Store::shardOf` (CityHash64(ref_name) % root_shards, for the owner journal). There are also two independent lease/watermark concepts: the GC lease inside `gc/state`, versus the mount lease / build watermark at `gc/server-roots/<srid>/mount`; `computeHeartbeatFloor` fences only the latter, never the GC lease.

There is no crash-resume step in the GC round: the whole round commits in the single `gc/state` CAS at the end, so a crashed pass leaves only attempt-scoped debris under its own unadopted lease.seq, never adopted and later reclaimed by `pruneSupersededGenerations` or the Task-7 hand-off. Every pre-CAS destructive action is justified by previously-published durable state (`delete_pending`), making replay under a fresh attempt idempotent.

`trim_enabled` in the GC scheduler is a test-only seam (production always runs with it true); `setTrimEnabledForTest`/`setRebuildEdgeBudgetForTest` exist only for tests. Scheduler config keys are `gc_interval`, `gc_fold_threshold`, `gc_fold_max_defer_rounds`, `gc_snap_generations_to_keep`, `gc_shards`, `gc_meta_pool_size`, `mount_lease_ttl_ms`, `manifest_sweep_{list,delete}_budget_keys`, `rebuild_edge_budget`; the heartbeat cadence is `hb_interval = max(50ms, interval/4)`.

`cleanupRefObjects` only deletes ref logs/snapshots that are covered by BOTH the durable fold cursor AND a durable snapshot; GC never invents a ref transition, and dead-precommit cleanup (appending exact owner_transition removals) is the writer's job, not GC's.

The orphan-manifest sweep gates deletion by `prefixEligible`, a durable watermark-only fact (`min_active > build_sequence`, or the retired sentinel `min_active==UINT64_MAX`, or an older epoch; a missing watermark means NOT eligible), and skips any key still in `activeManifestKeys(ns)` (committed + live precommits + manifests removed above the durable fold cursor). It never GETs a condemned body to revive it.

`SYSTEM ... GC` reuses the scheduler's existing `Gc` instance (a per-call one-shot would acquire the lease once then back off forever, since the steal protocol needs a stable gc_id); only the log record's Trigger differs (Manual vs scheduled). `SYSTEM ... GC REBUILD [FORCE]` instead constructs a one-shot `Gc` and calls `rebuildBaseline`, which recomputes the in-degree snapshot from raw owner state, mints numbering above every surviving ack, publishes a fresh seal, and CASes gc/state — it is live-conservative, fail-closed on refusals, and never deletes content.

Ref transaction IDs (`RefTxnId = {writer_epoch, ref_sequence}`) are strictly increasing with epoch as the primary component, so a recreated namespace always gets greater ids than a prior life — no ABA check is needed on ref-log ordering.

The controller's Task 5 removal design gives the smallest catalog state set as `Creating`, `Live`, `Removing`, `Retired` (four persisted states), where `Absent` is a lookup result rather than a persisted state, and `Decommissioning` is deliberately excluded as a namespace state — it is a server-root administrative mode that drives affected namespaces through the same four-state transitions rather than a fifth catalog state.

Loose mountpoint files are not namespaces — they are path-owned plain objects with conditional overwrite/exact deletion, drained by server-root decommission. Directory creation has no durable representation and creates no catalog row. Detached and moving parts are ref-name prefixes inside the owning table's namespace, not separate namespaces.

The ref catalog is a single raw token-CAS object capped at 256 MiB; admission is checked against both the encoded catalog byte size and a separate per-entry fold-seal reservation. A permanent never-deleted `Retired` history would eventually exhaust this cap, returning `LIMIT_EXCEEDED` on new namespace admission regardless of live cardinality — the GET/decode/encode/whole-object-CAS cost also grows with total historical births, not current live count.

On namespace decommission, catalog rows under the victim server_root_id are handled by state: `Live` rows go through normal removal, `Removing` rows resume, `Retired` rows are already done, and a `Creating` row may only be retired after its creator fence is terminal (since publication is forbidden while `Creating`, only a possibly-published `_ckpt` needs exact cleanup). Loose mountpoint and staging objects remain separate drains from namespace removal.

CAS should forbid the `Ordinary` database engine outright — its UUID-less `data/<db>/<tbl>` layout keeps a table's RootNamespace stable across drop-and-recreate, defeating the incarnation model — but this alone is insufficient: `ATTACH TABLE ... UUID '<same>'`, explicit-UUID `CREATE TABLE`, replicated-database DDL requiring UUID reuse, and shadow/backup namespace reuse (`FREEZE ... WITH NAME`) remain reachable exact-namespace-reuse routes that a forbid-Ordinary-only policy does not close.

STAGE B VERDICT (round 2, both reviewers converged): keep the namespace incarnation (option 2) rather than switching to permanent RootNamespace non-reuse or an outside-catalog retirement marker. Permanent non-reuse fails because shadow namespaces are reusable by construction and explicit-UUID attach/replicated-recovery reuse are supported workflows; a permanent `Retired` catalog state is the right shape only if retirement is wanted at all, but costs unbounded O(historical-namespaces) growth on the catalog, which is already a measured write hot spot (137/250 timeout lines).

With the incarnation kept, no namespace retirement bookkeeping is needed at all: removal ends in catalog entry deletion, debris becomes inert by foreign incarnation prefix, and the catalog stays O(active namespaces). The existing `_cleanup` marker that gates same-namespace recreation is identified as a Stage-A physical-empty vestige that the incarnation makes unnecessary and should be deleted, not carried into the new removal design.

The RemovalReady proposal leaves the `Removed` ref-snapshot's fate conditional even though it has a second consumer: `namespaceIsRemoved`'s cold-runtime recovery reads the `Removed` lifecycle state, which the reader-absence predicate rides on. The task must decide the mechanism explicitly: reader absence should come from the catalog cut, and the `Removed` snapshot plus the `_cleanup` gate should be rewired or deleted together.

The RemovalReady state costs less wire-format surface than a life-keyed-cursor alternative: cursor identity appears in eight files spanning the wire grammar, every builder/parser, REBUILD, fsck, and the sweep's coverage lookup, versus one enum value, one codec branch, one transition, and the five predicate sites for RemovalReady. Life-keyed cursors also create a new corner case (a reborn name's fresh-life cursor coexists with a dead-life cursor nothing prunes), so they only relocate the retirement-tracking problem rather than avoiding it.

For `ContentAddressedMetadataStorage`, the ctor default for `root_shards_` is 8 while the factory's config default is 32; a pool minted via the ctor default (e.g. in a unit test bypassing the factory) is stuck at fanout 8 because `root_shards` is creation-time-only.

`DiskObjectStorage::wrapWithCache` reuses the CA metadata storage directly instead of wrapping it in the generic `MetadataStorageFromCacheObjectStorage`, because the generic wrapper would hide `isContentAddressed()` and the concrete types the CA read/write paths `dynamic_cast` to, forcing the write path into `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`; only the object storage is cached, control-plane traffic bypasses the cache via the CA storage's own raw object-storage pointer.

CA namespace mapping: a detached part uses the same table namespace with ref `detached/<part>` (no parallel namespace, B181 fold); a FREEZE shadow uses the literal shadow table directory as namespace (bijective, pool-global); verbatim table-level files (`format_version.txt`, `deduplication_logs/…`, mutation entries) are namespace files; loose startup-probe files are plain mountpoint objects at `roots/<server_root_id>/<path>`.

`listDirectory`/`existsDirectory` branch by path shape in a fixed, load-bearing order — shadow, atomic-shard-dir, table-uuid, part-file, table-subdir, generic mirrored LIST — because `store/<u3>` and non-Atomic `data/<db>` would otherwise collide, so `isAtomicShardDir` must be consulted before `parseTableUuid`.

Mutable per-part files (`kMutablePerPartFiles`: `uuid.txt`, `txn_version.txt`, `metadata_version.txt`, plus `.tmp` siblings) live in `RefPayload.mutable_files`, never in the shared manifest tree, and are matched on the last path component only.

Every CAS key family is rooted at `POOL = pool_prefix`: blob body `POOL/blobs/<algo>/<S>/<hex>` (self-describing, `<S>`=first 2 hex chars); blob meta `POOL/blobs/<algo>/<S>/<hex>.meta`; part manifest `POOL/cas/manifests/<ns>/<epoch-hex>-<seq-hex>/<NNNNNN>.proto`; ref log txn `POOL/cas/refs/<ns>/_log/<render>`; ref snapshot `POOL/cas/refs/<ns>/_snap/<render>.proto`; ref cleanup marker `POOL/cas/refs/<ns>/_cleanup/<render>`; verbatim namespace file `POOL/roots/<ns>/_files/<name>`; plain mountpoint object `POOL/roots/<key>`; pool meta `POOL/_pool_meta`; GC state/heartbeat `POOL/gc/state`, `POOL/gc/hb`; GC generation artifacts `POOL/gc/gen/<gen>/attempt/<a>/...`; server-root control `POOL/gc/server-roots/<srid>/{owner,epoch,mount}`; opt-in staging `POOL/staging/<mount_id>/...` (a distinct top-level sibling GC never LISTs).

`blobsPrefix()` deliberately stays `POOL/blobs/` with no algo segment so a single recursive LIST returns every algo; strict key parsers (`parseBlobKey`, `parseManifestKey`, `parseRefObjectKey`) return `std::nullopt` (never throw) for foreign/malformed keys, treating them as debris rather than corruption.

`CasEnvelope` is a 70-byte little-endian core header (magic, writer_version, compatibility_version, hash_algo, flags, header_len, domain_id[16], incarnation_tag[16], build_id[16], header_hash[8]) followed by TLV extensions padded to a per-pool fixed `header_len`, so blob payloads always start at a constant offset for a constant-shift `locate`; `logical_size`/`logical_hash` core fields were dropped 2026-07-11 to let the header be built before the payload streams (S3-native staging).

`CasBlobMeta` (the `.meta` freshness sibling) is a fixed `CAMT`-magic codec with `BODY_LEN=22` (magic[4]+version[1]+state[1]+condemn_round[8 LE]+size[8 LE]); `version` must equal 1 and `state` must be Clean=0 or Condemned=1, else decode fail-closes.

`CasPoolMeta` (`_pool_meta`) is a pure protobuf `PoolMetaProto` holding `pool_id`, `root_shards`, `blob_header_len`, `min_reader_generation`, and a sorted append-only `algos_used[]`; invariants are `root_shards >= 1` and `blob_header_len` 8-aligned in `[96, 16384]`; admitting a new hash algorithm raises `min_reader_generation` to `G_BUILD` in the same CAS.

`CasManifestCodec` (`CAPT` magic) encodes `format_version`, `writer_version`, `ref{epoch,seq,ordinal}`, the namespace, a `payload_digest` (integrity/debug only, never a key/dedup/in-degree input), and entries as an embedded RunFile keyed by path; the decoder enforces strict ascending canonical path order and rejects duplicate paths, an invariant `findEntry`/`entryRange` binary search relies on.

Plain-object CAS loops (`casPutObject`/`casRemoveObject`, used for namespace files and mountpoint objects) run through the backend's default retry policy rather than `CasRequestController`, so they get no single-attempt client and no lease-relative deadline — bounded only by a local `MAX_CAS_ATTEMPTS=100` — meaning a flaky S3 could let such a write outlive the mount lease, the exact hazard the RFC timeout model forbids for the ref lane.

The removal driver resumes entry deletion idempotently on the owning writer's next mount after a stop in the `Removing`-without-`_ckpt` window; it never re-creates `_ckpt`, and the dead-root branch belongs to the decommission path instead.

Under strict removal ordering, the worst cases "two cleanup rows for one namespace" and "a cleanup row with no catalog entry" become unconstructible (both require rebirth before the first removal retired); the worst-case capacity test should be replaced by an anomaly check that fires if GC ever observes an entry-less cleanup row.

Blocking issue: cursor pruning is not monotone across crash-resume — if the process stops after the pruned seal is durable but before `_ckpt`/entry deletion, the catalog still shows `Removing`, and a later GC round adds every `Live`/`Removing` entry back to `walk_targets` and writes a cursor for it, reintroducing the pruned cursor; the resumed removal driver then has no safe-and-live choice between trusting the historical pruned seal or waiting on the current seal indefinitely.

Probe A detects CAS ref-prefix LIST incompleteness via two independent enumerations per GC round (the pre-fold defer scan and fold's own enumeration); it compares per-namespace id sets and reports a hole only when the id is below the OTHER enumeration's own maximum for that namespace, which excludes ordinary in-flight appends between the two walks.

Probe A has two documented blind spots it does not catch: a hole that reproduces identically in both enumerations, and a namespace dropped wholesale from one enumeration (no `ref_tables` entry, so the comparison loop never visits it); widening the witness rule to use the pre-scan's own maximum was considered and rejected because it would permanently block the cursor on a namespace whose logs were legitimately cleaned between the walks.

GC's `fold_ref_intake` is linear in the ref-log backlog at 256 logs/s sustained; the flat cost is per S3 request (~0.92 ms), decomposing as one GET per log body plus one per emitted manifest edge, so round trips equal `logs + 2*edges`, and edges-per-log climbs from 1.54 to 3.73 as backlog grows.

39.6% of GC intake manifest fetches are re-reads (7,565 edges over 4,573 distinct manifests): intra-transaction redundancy is exactly zero, and all of it is cross-transaction (2,991 manifests carry both an add and a remove edge in the window, so the same body is read once when the ref is published and again when it is dropped), making a round-scoped body cache — not an op- or transaction-scoped one — the effective lever.

The chosen fix (Fix 4) for the deposed-leader stray-Clean defect makes GC freshness metadata add-only: GC never transitions Condemned to Clean on a spare (the spare-side `clearSparedMeta` call and helper are removed); only a writer that has displaced the body with a fresh incarnation token publishes Clean, via `uploadFromSource` + `writeResurrectMetaClean`/`copyForwardFromCondemned`. Accepted cost: a spared hash stays Condemned until a writer resurrects it (write amplification on recurring-hash churn); normal reads never consult the meta so this is safe.

The first proposed fix for the deposed-leader stray-Clean defect (Fix 1: couple `clearSparedMeta` to adoption by moving it after the winning `gc/state` CAS, plus a `condemn_round` guard) was proven insufficient by a second model consult: a stale, paused leader can issue the destructive exact-token `deleteExact(t1)` pre-CAS from an older adopted snapshot, so a fresh leader's legitimately-adopted post-CAS clear still lets a writer reuse `t1` and the stale leader's redelete kills the live reuse, because the final `gc/state` CAS fences adoption, not pre-CAS side effects.

`clearSparedMeta` (`Core/CasGc.cpp:106-113`) clears a blob's freshness meta from Condemned to Clean when a GC round spares it, scheduled on the spare verdict and completed BEFORE the round's single `gc/state` CAS; a GC leader that runs it and then loses the CAS leaves a durable stray-Clean meta over a blob still `delete_pending` in the durably-adopted run. Stray-Clean is the unsafe direction (unlike stray-Condemned, which only costs an unnecessary resurrect) because it defeats the writer's freshness gate, letting a writer reuse the exact condemned incarnation token; a later pending exact-token redelete then deletes the live reused incarnation.

Restricting a deposed GC leader's advisory meta to condemn-only (add-only, never clearing to Clean) makes the TLA+ witness model GREEN (935,815 distinct states), confirming that stray-Condemned effects are safe as the v3 spec claims and that the SOLE violation source was the stray-Clean `clearSparedMeta`; `FoldRound`'s identical clean-on-spare write is safe only because it is coupled to adoption (the pending row is dropped in the same atomic step), a coupling the deposed-leader case lacks.

Lesson recorded from the deposed-leader stray-Clean investigation: a formal model that is safer than the code hides real bugs. The original `CaRetiredInRun` TLA gate did not model the deposed leader and stayed green; a first attempted fix made the model advisory-add-only and also went green, but this was a false-green that masked the code's actual behavior (`clearSparedMeta` really does clear-to-Clean pre-CAS) until the BLOCKED verdict and a not-weaken-invariants discipline caught the discrepancy.

The CAS merge-layout preparation's top identified risk (R1) is that an extraction changes lock discipline: the publish lane's correctness depends on the two-phase carve happening under one continuous lock hold and the install region not allocating; the mitigation is to extract only pure functions called from the same place under the same lock (so discipline is unchanged by construction) and to gate on a soak run, not just gtests.

The CAS merge-layout preparation's R2 risk is `Pool` facade churn, since B6 touches the class everything depends on; the mitigation is to do that extraction last and keep `Pool` as a delegating facade so call sites are untouched.

The CAS merge-layout preparation's R3 risk is that `docs/superpowers/cas/11-walkthrough.md` cites roughly 200 file:line references that workstream B invalidates; the mitigation is to refresh the walkthrough as the final step of workstream B, before carving, since it is the document reviewers read first.

The CAS merge-layout preparation's R4 risk is that workstream A3 may be reshaped in upstream review after it has already landed in the fork; the mitigation is to keep A3's fork commits identical to what is proposed upstream and treat upstream feedback as a follow-up to both.

The CAS merge-layout preparation's R5 risk is calendar: roughly 20-25 PRs; the mitigation relies on the workstream parallelism plus keeping unit PRs small (200-600 lines) to keep review latency per PR low.

The CAS merge-layout preparation left open decision D1 (granularity) unresolved: the proposal is fine-grained, one complex algorithm per PR (about 20-25 PRs) relying on workstream parallelism, versus the alternative of eight medium PRs of about 5-6k lines each.

The CAS merge-layout preparation left open decision D2 (sequencing of workstream B) unresolved: the proposal is to complete all of workstreams B and C before carving, versus the alternative of carving each hot spot as soon as it is extracted, which gets reviewer feedback earlier but keeps the working branch alive longer and risks divergence.

The CAS merge-layout preparation left open decision D3 unresolved: whether the extracted units should live in new sub-directories (for example `Gc/Round/`, `Pool/Ref/`) or keep the current flat per-layer layout with more files.

The ack-floor GC redesign drops `process_epoch` as a separate merged-heartbeat field because the writable path already sets `process_epoch = writer_epoch` (`CasStore.cpp:157`) and the sweep consumes `writer_epoch` unchanged, so a distinct field would be redundant.

The ack-floor design renamed the sabotage control `SabotageDeleteAtFloor` to `SabotageIgnoreAckFloor` because an `r < min_ack` vs `r ≤ min_ack` off-by-one is provably still safe under the publish-order invariant, so the load-bearing control is "ignores the floor entirely", not the exact boundary.

The source-layout refactor's phase-5 rename sweep (`Store`→`Pool`, `Build`→`PartWriteTxn`) must use word-boundary-anchored seds rather than blanket `s/Store/.../` or `s/Build/.../`, because a blanket substitution would incorrectly hit `IMetadataStorage` and the protocol vocabulary `build_seq`/`BuildPrefix`, which must survive the rename unchanged.

A codex review of the publish-confirm/ref-lane-safety landing raised three footprint objections against the upstream-coupling-minimization rule; two were knowingly accepted as tradeoffs and recorded as accepted (not debt) rather than corrected: `DataPartsExchange.h` exposing `allow_ca_relink` and CAS-specific service helpers beyond the opaque enum, and the confirm/relink logic spanning more functions per side than the rule's ideal shape.

A reviewer's objection that the `src/Common/ProfileEvents.cpp` registration exceeded the approved failpoint scope was refuted as a conflation: the registration came from a separate task, not the failpoint-approval task, and a `ProfileEvent` registration is not protocol coupling; the failpoint approval's actual scope (only `src/Common/FailPoint.cpp` registration lines) was exercised exactly as recorded.

The publish-confirm/ref-lane-safety design deliberately uses two distinct types for the same confirm answer across the exchange boundary — `ConfirmAnswer` in the ledger and `CasConfirmAnswer` in the exchange wire header, and `PreparedPartWrite` (CAS-internal) exposed through the abstract `ICaPreparedRelink` — so that `DataPartsExchange.cpp` needs no CAS-internal headers, keeping the one type mapping confined to a single implementation file.

The ref-lease-exclusivity rev.6 proposal left four open questions for review at draft time: whether a 30s `T_mat` unclean-handover penalty is acceptable in production given rustfs/MinIO/real-S3 request-lifetime differences; whether the eager recovery snapshot should also run on clean mounts with a large inherited tail; whether the seal's wedge/single-in-flight invariant may be hard-required via chassert plus release fail-close at the lane level; and confirming that the interim mechanical patch (aged trigger, copy-once replay, threshold 256) lands regardless of the proposal's outcome.

The relink protocol's defense against an actively-forged affirmative confirm answer relies on the request/response shape being structurally opaque to caches, not on cache policy alone: both legs are POST (not cacheable absent freshness metadata that is never sent), `Cache-Control: no-store` (not `no-cache`) is pinned on both responses to forbid storage entirely rather than permit storage-with-revalidation, and interserver authentication runs before the shared handler dispatches to any endpoint.
Phase 2 pluggable-hash `sha256` blobs are stored under the key shape `blobs/sha256/<shard>/<64-hex>`, distinct from the default 128-bit hash's `blobs/<aa>/<H>` layout.

Under the one-pipeline transaction design, CA manifest build, blob upload, and promote (remote I/O) deliberately run inside `MergeTreeData::Transaction::commit` under `lockParts()` (`MergeTreeData.cpp:8775/8792`); this is an accepted tradeoff per the spec's `Why There Is No Disk Precommit` rationale, not a regression, since moving remote I/O out of `data_parts` locking is a general commit-positioning/performance problem, not a CA-only correctness issue.

The condemned-evidence copy-forward design has a queued (not-yet-executed) validation task: a fresh soak run on a clean pool replaying the S13-adjacent kill-restart chaos, with the attach path expected to recover — verified by grepping for `BlobCopyForward` events and confirming zero "table will remain readonly" occurrences without recovery.

The source-layout refactoring design defers a backlog of deliberately-not-done improvements: a constructor config struct for the pool facade's ~25 positional parameters, flattening `SingleWriterSlot` into `MountLeaseKeeper` if no second subclass appears, and retiring vestiges like `ShardIncarnation` and the unreachable `CasNs::Server`.

Stage-B has two non-gating follow-ups scheduled after the T9 closeout: F1, a post-baseline mechanical split of `CasGc.cpp` and `CasRefLedger.cpp` along existing seams (request-count/order goldens captured before and rerun unchanged after); and F2, pre-upstream sanitation that strips branch-local documentation references and coordination markers from production code while keeping each rationale, starting from a measured 76-reference comment inventory and remeasuring before declaring it clean.

The GC-rebuild validation plan (queued outside this plan) is: mid-soak `mc rm` of `gc/state` should make the guard's `CORRUPTED_DATA` appear in the GC round log with `outcome='Error'` and nothing deleted afterward, then `SYSTEM CONTENT ADDRESSED GC REBUILD` on one replica should let rounds resume and fsck converge to `dangling=0` with `pending-gc` draining.
The S3-native staging plan's memory fast-path (spec §7) is explicitly deferred out of the plan as a separable optimization, noted for a follow-on.

The reftable COW-map plan's self-review found the actual access-site inventory for `RefTableState::committed` was 18 sites across 5 files (verified against the tree), not the ~15 sites the spec estimated; all but one site was a drop-in change.

The S42/GC-perf overnight study plan is diagnostic-only: no task in the plan implements a fix, the only contemplated code changes are a counter or a log line, and none is required by the plan's tasks.

The ack-floor GC redesign explicitly defers delta-runs plus compaction for the snapshot (amortizing snapshot bytes to O(edges) per pass instead of O(universe)) as follow-on streaming work, expected to become the next bottleneck after the redesign lands.
The ack-floor GC redesign leaves `process_epoch` to `writer_epoch` unification as a follow-up, since it touches manifest `writer_instance_id` stamps and is out of scope for this design.
The ack-floor GC redesign leaves adaptive per-namespace `root_shards` (a universe-size-reduction knob) as an orthogonal follow-up, out of scope for this design.

The TXN-ONE-PIPELINE design flags a candidate upstream issue in its Backlog Observation: on plain object storage, carried-forward projections can be absent from an in-memory mutated part until reload, because queued hardlinks are invisible to `loadProjections`; fixing ordinary object-storage read-your-writes is explicitly outside the design's scope.

The TXN-ONE-PIPELINE design's plan-time audits require a fault-injection regression verifying that process termination after a successful `Keeper` publication but before disk `commit` enters the existing missing-part fetch/lost-part path, and explicitly forbid introducing CA-specific recovery for this window.

The TXN-ONE-PIPELINE design's plan-time audits require re-evaluating the empty-covering-part `commitTransaction` workaround before deleting it, since moving publication into `commit` does not automatically make the workaround redundant.

The branch-reconstruction carve script accepts, as a residual risk, that a file moved between source areas (e.g. a gtest moved into a layer directory) silently changes which commit carries it; this is accepted because the commit grouping is presentational only.

GCS generation binding's OAuth leg (`gcp_oauth` dialect with ADC credentials) is deliberately not implemented as a task because no ADC credentials exist on the validation stand; it is tracked only as a ROADMAP row, not gated on.
The ref-table snapshot-log Phase 1 plan has zero deliberate deviations from its spec; Phase 2 items are excluded per the plan's Global Constraints, not silently dropped.
Codex triage finding №18 was not given its own task because the root fix in Task 2 collapses it; the affected list-branch change is called out explicitly inside Task 2 rather than as a separate item.

In the CAS mount-fence write-grace plan, no test may `EXPECT_THROW` a `LOGICAL_ERROR`; Part B failure paths must surface as `INVALID_STATE` or `NETWORK_ERROR`, which are safe to assert with `EXPECT_THROW` under sanitizers.

For the mount-fence rev.2 silent-expiry path, Mode 2 coverage rests on the `setMountDeadline` signaler plus the Mode-2 ride-out test; the signaler is the load-bearing addition, since without it Part B never wakes on the dominant (silent-expiry) path.

The CAS mount-fence write-grace feature introduces the settings/metrics `write_grace_ms`, `waitForWriteGrace`, `CasMountFenceArmed`, `CasSelfRemountCompleted`, `CasSelfRemountMicroseconds`, `CasMountFenceExpired`, `CasMountFenceExpiredMicroseconds`, `fence_tripped_boot_ms`, and `fence_expiry_reported_boot_ms`.

The docs consolidation project's own risk register names four risks and mitigations: docs describing a moving target (mitigated by HEAD-time verification and an experimental-format banner), false done/stale verdicts losing knowledge (mitigated by an evidence requirement plus a sampled adversarial audit at Gate M), map agents summarizing instead of extracting claims (mitigated by a one-claim-per-record rule and the Gate M missed-claim audit), and new docs bloating back into walls of text (mitigated by a per-page style gate with a volume limit and a diagonal-reading review test).

An optional pre-pass refresh for the promote copy-forward tokenless-blob race fix (spec §3) was deliberately deferred rather than implemented: it is a fast-path-only optimization, not required for correctness, so it was left unscheduled rather than turned into a task.
A thread-local "active slot" design for the part-folder cache was rejected as unnecessary v1 complexity with no measurable benefit over a bounded shared map lookup.

Reducing admits() call frequency (backlog fix #2) was rejected as an alternative to the incremental-counter design because each remaining call would still be O(N), and reducing call frequency changes per-operation validation granularity (a later op in a batch is currently validated against state reflecting earlier ops in the same batch), which would need its own separate safety review; it is lateral on cost and weaker on safety than the chosen incremental-counter approach.

For the incremental ref-ledger byte counters, `RefTableState` equality/hashing in tests is safe only because the counters are a pure function of the rows (any two states with equal rows have equal counters); the residual risk to verify is that no test constructs a `RefTableState` with populated rows outside the two designated seeding paths.

For the CAS naming-unification migration, old `content_addressed`/`ca` names embedded in many `.reference` test files must be changed in the same commit as the corresponding code change; correctness for this migration is checked by grep review of user-facing surfaces, not by running the stateless test suite.

The CAS naming-unification migration's identified risks include possible undetected persistence of the old metadata storage type string (see the design's Scope §4) and the CAS-related tag rename needing to stay in sync across tests, the test runner, the CI job definition, and the Claude skills that reference it.
The writer-GC-simplification Phase A plan deliberately leaves Phase B (further simplification) out of this plan, to be written as a separate plan after a meta-consult.
The introspection-first plan's spec item §0.4 is deliberately left unimplemented in this plan; it lands later together with the opt-in levers work once the spec is amended (commit ace3549b071+).

The umbrella-review-fixes plan explicitly leaves report findings 1 and 6 unaddressed (deferred by user instruction / covered by an existing separate plan) and finding 11 unaddressed because it is an upstream-process issue rather than a code fix.

Whether `ApplyPending` can later become debug-only is recorded as a follow-up but deliberately not implemented in the Stage-B catalog plan; `RefApplyState` refactoring is out of scope per Constraint 17.

A wrapper type for "life captured at admission" (which would make the finalize-lambda life-capture type-checkable) was deliberately rejected as over-engineering for a single call site in the Stage-B catalog work; the delayed-writer-finalized test is the only guard against a silent regression there and must not be dropped or weakened.

The ideal, fully-invisible zero-re-upload fix for the promote/GC condemn race is a writer-triggerable synchronous fold that activates the precommit edge before revalidation, but no writer↔GC synchronous-fold API exists today (only a test-only foldManifestEdgesForTest); this is recorded as a follow-up, with the bounded in-closure resurrect used as the pragmatic fix instead.

Accepting a condemned tokened blob without resurrecting it is UNSOUND and rejected in the promote/resurrect design, because the condemn→delete pipeline is exact-token two-phase and an accepted-but-condemned token can graduate to delete, dangling the manifest; only a fresh incarnation via uploadFromSource is safe.

Widening the CAS GC-log to carry mount state was deliberately NOT done as part of the introspection package (design: YAGNI) because the new `system.content_addressed_mounts` table already carries the needed point-in-time mount state.

The `RefTableState` closed-class experiments round's success criterion (Task 8 final gate) is: after a 20-minute soak, the hottest CAS-attributed CPU stack family in the `trace_log` profile must be blob hashing, and every other CAS-attributed family must be at most one third of blob hashing's sample count; a miss turns the residual hotspot into a new experiment row rather than closing the round.

The ref-chain v9 TLA+ phase deliberately does not model the temporal lemma's writer-side arms (condemned-meta rematerialization, tokenless relink ordering); those are treated as existing-code properties verified by the main plan's C++ tests, recorded as a scope note rather than a modeling gap.

Open question from the mount-lease self-race fix proposal: whether the existing `ProfileEvents::CasMountLeaseLost` counter (already incremented by `superseded`/`foreign_writer`/`vanished`) should semantically absorb the new self-raced-renewal case or warrant its own more specific counter, mirroring the `CasGcRetiredSparedByReref` split tracked under BACKLOG item `RECOVERED-INDEGREE-ATTRIBUTION`.

In the meta-descriptor raw-body plan, the absent-meta AND absent-body retry mechanism in putBlob's step (Task 3 step 5) is left as an open implementation choice between a sentinel value and a re-throw-ABORTED-and-retry approach; whichever is picked, putBlob and observeAndAdmitByMeta must stay consistent.

The delete ThreadPool sizing (gc_delete_pool_size) for the meta-descriptor raw-body redesign starts at a default of 16 and is left to be validated/tuned by the soak task (Task 7 step 4), not fixed at design time.

An early draft of the relink/seam TLA+ model omitted the WedgeRetryCreated action entirely, making the wedge protocol's own happy path unreachable: CasRefLedger.h:784-801 documents that a bounded conditional-create retry either lands the exact same transaction bytes or conflicts, so without modelling that retry as a durability-producing event, WedgeResolveInstall's sApplyOwed guard could never be satisfied and every state downstream of a resolved wedge was missing from the state space.

A later draft of the relink/seam TLA+ model omitted FloorReconcile entirely while leaving WedgeResolveInstall enabled on sWedge /\ sApplyOwed, which admitted a poisoned-to-clean install as reachable when it should be impossible; a blanket ~sWedge exclusion in MarkerCoversDurableWindow was rejected because it hid the bug rather than describing the code — once the invariant's subject became the mount's own owed apply, no exclusion was needed for either the wedge or the fence.

The relink/seam TLA+ model deliberately introduces three controls the spec does not name (_ctl_v11nomarker, _ctl_distinctns, _ctl_skipidentity) because a flip with no control would be a coincidence and a green with no scoping statement would be a silent gap; it also models the full wedge lifecycle (hazards and happy path) beyond what section 12 of the spec asks for, because three drafts proved that modelling rule 3 without the wedge lifecycle produced sabotages that were red for unreachable states and greens resting on missing ones.

In the CAS GC-observability skipped-transaction-detector design, probe A's independence from probe B rests on the two enumerations being separate physical LIST walks; if a future optimisation merges them (listing the same prefix twice is an obvious target), probe A would silently become vacuous, and the design leaves open whether the guard against this should be a code comment forbidding the merge or a test asserting two distinct LIST walks occur.

Probe B's throw wedges GC until an operator runs the rebuild; on a pre-release soak stand this cost a disk-budget blowout, with the last observed run reclaiming 124 GB at one checkpoint once the wedge was cleared, which motivates the open question of whether the first N occurrences should suppress-and-continue with a counter, escalating to a throw only on recurrence.

In the CAS GC per-phase observability row design, phase_metrics is typed as a Map, so there is no compile-time type checking on key names and a typo in a key is invisible; the design leaves open whether this is worth a compile-time key list or is over-engineering for an introspection table.

The CAS GC per-phase row design treats its 17-phase split as a judgement call: fold_seal_read and fold_seal_write (one GET and one PUT) could fold into neighbouring phases, and round_commit mixes the heavy prune step with the trivial CAS step and arguably should be split.

In the CAS GC per-phase observability design, fsck_pre and fsck_post are each asserted clean individually but are never compared structurally against each other, despite an existing code comment promising such a comparison — a named, deliberately-unfixed gap rather than an oversight.

For the mount force-claim design, an overwrite force-claim permanently reassigns the pool's identity: the original server, on its next start, is refused by claimOwnerOrThrow and cannot mount its own root without manual recovery, and the error message it receives (CasServerRoot.cpp:125-131) misleadingly blames a regenerated local uuid file. A cheaper alternative already exists in the codebase — Pool::openForDecommission (CasPool.cpp:720-776) impersonates the existing owner uuid instead of overwriting it, preserving pool identity so the original server can return, at the cost of two processes then presenting the same owner uuid (exactly what the mount lease exists to serialise). The plan implements overwrite (per the literal decision) but isolates the choice to one function so switching to impersonation is a small edit; which to use is left as an open, user-facing decision, not an implementation detail.

The mount force-claim design leaves open whether a forced mount should also refuse to start the GC scheduler, so that a diagnostic tool taking ownership cannot also start reclaiming; the stated decision ("mounts as WRITE") argues no, while the blast radius of a diagnostic tool triggering GC argues yes.

PR #2073's sanitizer-abort plan deliberately leaves `SilkFiberSocketTest/1` unaddressed; if it later blocks a CI lane it must be escalated as a separate Altinity silk-fiber/sanitizer triage rather than folded into this fix.

Stage-B follow-up Task F1 (outside the Stage-B verdict) is a purely mechanical split of `CasGc.cpp` and `CasRefLedger.cpp` (each ~4000 lines) along their existing semantic seams (GC: phases/fold/janitor; ledger: writer lanes/recovery/publication), gated by request-count/order equivalence goldens captured before any code moves and rerun unchanged afterward — no lifecycle or runtime boundary redesign.

Stage-B follow-up Task F2 (before upstreaming) is a sanitation sweep that strips branch-local references (task/review/finding numbers, BACKLOG, "superpowers") from production code and operator-visible strings, keeping the underlying reason but deleting the citation, verified by `git grep` measuring the baseline (~76 references) down to zero.

The stabilization-cleanup design's item A2 (widening CRC coverage) alters the on-disk run-file framing; this is accepted pre-release on the condition that writer and reader are updated together and old-format run files are never expected to survive, since run files are attempt-scoped and short-lived.

`write_grace_ms` is independent of `cas_request_budget.operation_deadline_ms`, so a large grace plus a long remount can exceed a client's own request timeout; this is accepted because the client's own timeout then bounds the wait, and operators should size `write_grace_ms` near one lease TTL as the natural ceiling.
